title: Social Security, worked out
teaches: How the benefit is worked out from 35 years of earnings and the bend points, what stopping work early costs, how claiming age changes it, survivors' benefits, and delay as the cheapest inflation-linked income

parts.title: The largest asset most people own

blocks.text: A couple who will receive $50,000 a year of Social Security from 67 own something worth a great deal: an income that rises with prices every year, lasts as long as either of them lives, and is backed by the federal government. Buying the same thing from an insurer, if anyone sold it, would cost well over $1 million. For most retired households Social Security is the largest single source of income, and for many it is worth more than all their savings.

It is also the part of a plan with the most choices left in it. When to claim, which spouse claims when, and how many years of work count can change a household's lifetime benefits by hundreds of thousands of dollars. This lesson works through the formula and the choices.[^simple]

The benefit starts from your earnings history, up to the yearly cap, $184,500 in 2026. Each year's earnings are indexed to wage growth, the 35 highest are averaged, and the total is divided by 420 months to give average indexed monthly earnings, the AIME. Fewer than 35 years of work means zeros in the average.

The AIME goes through a formula with two bend points, which for someone turning 62 in 2026 are $1,286 and $7,749. The benefit at full retirement age is 90 percent of the AIME up to the first, 32 percent of the part between them, and 15 percent of the rest. The formula replaces most of a low earner's wages and a small share of a high earner's. Guess first.

blocks.caption: The monthly benefit at full retirement age (67) by average monthly earnings over 35 years, in today's dollars. The circle marks working all 35 years at the same earnings.
blocks.task: Guess, then compare 35 years of work with 15 or fewer

blocks.text: Someone who earns $150,000 a year for 20 years and then stops has 15 zeros in the average, which cuts their AIME by 43 percent. Their benefit falls only 23 percent, because the zeros come out of the 15 percent slice first. A high earner's last fifteen years of work add little to Social Security. A low earner's add much more, since their extra dollars would land in the 90 and 32 percent slices.

For anyone planning to stop work early, that's reassuring: the benefit at 67 is mostly earned by the mid-forties for a high earner. It's worth getting a real estimate from my Social Security at ssa.gov, which shows your record and projects the benefit if you stop now.

Benefits can start at any age from 62 to 70. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. Claim at 62 and the benefit is cut to 70 percent of the full amount, for life. Wait past 67 and it rises by 8 percent a year, to 124 percent at 70. So a benefit claimed at 70 is 77 percent larger than the same person's benefit at 62, and it rises with prices either way.

blocks.caption: Total benefits received by each age of death, claiming at 62, 67 or 70, in today's dollars. Slide the claiming age to compare others.

blocks.text: Waiting to 70 overtakes claiming at 62 for anyone who lives past about 80, and claiming at 67 at about 79. A 62-year-old's life expectancy is in the mid-eighties, so on average waiting pays, and it pays most in the case that matters most, a long life. Claiming early makes sense for someone in poor health, or a single person who needs the money and has no other way to bridge.

Before full retirement age, a claimant who is still working has benefits withheld: $1 for every $2 of earnings above $24,480 in 2026. The money isn't lost, since the benefit is raised later to make up for it, but it makes claiming early while working pointless for most.

A spouse can claim a benefit of up to half the other's full benefit, if that's more than their own, though not before the other has claimed, and with no extra for waiting past 67. More important for planning: when one spouse dies, the survivor keeps the larger of the two benefits and the smaller stops.

That makes the higher earner's claiming age a decision about the survivor's income. If the higher earner waits to 70, the larger benefit lasts as long as either of them lives, and for a couple in their sixties there are close to even odds that one reaches 90. A common plan has the lower earner claim earlier, at 62 to 67, and the higher earner wait to 70.
Divorced spouses married at least ten years can claim on an ex-spouse's record too, without affecting the ex-spouse's benefit.

Waiting from 62 to 70 means spending more from savings for eight years, in exchange for a larger income for life. Seen that way, delay is the purchase of an inflation-linked annuity, and a cheap one: each year of delay past 67 buys 8 percent more benefit for a year of benefits forgone, a better rate than any insurer offers.

It fits the rest of the course. The years before Social Security starts are low-income years, the ones lesson 10 fills with Roth conversions; once benefits start, the torpedo from lesson 12 makes the same conversions dearer. And a larger guaranteed income lowers the risk lesson 3 described: the portfolio has less to do later, so a bad sequence hurts less.

One risk is political. The 2025 Trustees Report projects that the trust funds will run out in 2034, after which incoming payroll taxes would cover about 81 percent of scheduled benefits.[^trust] Congress has always acted before such a date in the past, but a cautious plan for someone now in their forties or fifties might assume a cut of a fifth, and check how much it matters.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The benefit comes from the 35 highest years of indexed earnings, through slices replacing 90, 32 and 15 percent.
Stopping work early costs a high earner less than you'd expect, because the zeros come out of the 15 percent slice first.
Claiming at 70 pays 77 percent more a month than at 62, and overtakes it for anyone living past about 80.
A survivor keeps the larger benefit, so the higher earner's delay protects whichever spouse lives longer.

blocks.caption: Six questions on Social Security
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How many years of earnings does the benefit formula average?
choices: The highest 35, with zeros for missing years
items.why: The 35 highest years of indexed earnings are averaged; fewer years of work mean zeros in the average.

items.ask: Why does stopping work after 20 years cut a high earner's benefit by much less than 43 percent?
choices: The zeros come out of the part of the formula that replaces only 15 percent
Benefits are based on the last five years
The government adds credits for missing years
items.why: Lower AIME removes dollars from the top slice first, where each dollar of earnings adds only 15 cents of benefit.

items.ask: Compared with claiming at 62, how much larger is a benefit claimed at 70, for someone whose full retirement age is 67?
items.why: 70 percent of the full benefit at 62 against 124 percent at 70: 1.24 ÷ 0.70 is about 1.77.

items.ask: When one spouse dies, what happens to the couple's two benefits?
choices: The survivor keeps the larger and the smaller stops
items.why: The survivor benefit is the larger of the two, which is why the higher earner's claiming age matters for the survivor.

items.ask: A 63-year-old claims while still earning $44,480 in 2026. About how much is withheld?
items.why: $1 for every $2 above $24,480: half of $20,000. It is paid back later through a higher benefit.

items.ask: What does the 2025 Trustees Report project after 2034 if Congress does nothing?
choices: About 81 percent of scheduled benefits can be paid
items.why: Payroll taxes keep coming in after the trust funds run out, enough to pay most, but not all, of scheduled benefits.

summary: **Social Security is a large asset.** Inflation-linked income for life, worth more than many households' savings.
**Thirty-five years, three slices.** The highest 35 years of indexed earnings, replaced at 90, 32 and 15 percent across the bend points.
**Early stopping costs high earners little.** Twenty years at $150,000 instead of 35 cuts the benefit by about a quarter.
**Claiming age moves the benefit 77 percent.** 70 percent of the full amount at 62, 124 percent at 70.
**Waiting pays for a long life.** Claiming at 70 overtakes 62 for anyone living past about 80.
**The survivor keeps the larger benefit.** The higher earner waiting protects whichever spouse lives longer.
**Delay is cheap inflation-linked income.** And the years before claiming are good years for Roth conversions.

simple.title: What the figures leave out
simple.text: The course's version of the formula treats past earnings as already in today's dollars. The real one indexes each year's earnings to national wage growth up to age 60, uses the bend points of the year you turn 62, and rounds at several steps. The results are close, but use the estimate on your own record for real planning.

trust.title: The trust funds
trust.text: Social Security has been paid mostly from current payroll taxes since 1940. Surpluses from the 1980s to the 2010s, when the baby boom was working, were lent to the Treasury and built up the trust funds, which are now being drawn down as that generation retires. The last large fix, in 1983, raised the retirement age from 65 to 67 in stages and began taxing benefits.
